paras: The threatened lynching of Edward Alberson and James Eato took place at the railroad depot in Roslyn, Long Island, New York, on the night of March 25, 1882, when a crowd threatened to lynch the two Black prisoners as officers removed them to the Queens County Jail. The officers got the men onto the train, and both later stood trial in Long Island City. The threat appears in a single New-York Tribune report on a robbery case that the paper followed closely.

On the night of Tuesday, March 21, William M. Valentine, a 73-year-old Roslyn merchant, was struck on the head near his home and robbed of about twelve dollars. He was found unconscious with a fractured skull, and physicians gave little hope of his recovery. The next day officers arrested Edward Alberson, described as "a negro" and "a wandering vagabond" whose boot was said to fit one set of footprints.

James Eato, also identified as a Black man, was arrested on March 23 after his shoes were said to match the second set of tracks. Justice Losee arraigned both men and committed them to the Roslyn lockup to await the outcome of Valentine's injuries, while neighbors posted a $450 reward. The Tribune reported that the men's guilt was not doubted locally.

On the night of March 25 the two prisoners were taken from Roslyn to the Queens County Jail in Long Island City. According to the Tribune, "a crowd gathered at the Roslyn depot when they left and threatened to lynch them." The Sheriff's officers had "great difficulty" getting the men onto the cars safely, and no seizure or injury was reported. The size of the crowd and the names of its members were not given.

Deputies reported on March 30 that Eato had confessed in his cell, naming Albertson, his cousin, as the man who struck the blow, and had led them to Valentine's pocketbook hidden in his cellar. Prosecutors decided to take the case directly to the Grand Jury, and the men's statements were taken down in writing. No arrest or prosecution of anyone in the crowd at the depot is reported in the coverage.

The trial began on July 10 in the Queens County Court of Sessions in Long Island City, where Eato was granted a separate trial. On July 13 a jury found Albertson guilty of assaulting Valentine, but the report breaks off before his sentence, and no verdict for Eato was found.

Coverage came almost entirely from the New-York Tribune, which ran items on the case from March 23 through July 14. The paper reported the lynch threat in two sentences, without comment, within an item on Valentine's improving health headed "Removed to the Queens County Jail." Its earlier reports called the suspects "negroes" of "evil reputation" and printed the officers' and the victim's son's certainty of their guilt before any hearing.

Out-of-town papers carried only short briefs on the robbery: the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer printed a Flushing wire naming no suspects, and the Portland Daily Press reported Eato's confession. Neither brief mentioned the threat at the depot.
The Portland Daily Press brief said Valentine had recovered, while the Tribune's later local reports described him as comatose and failing.

accounts.label: New-York Tribune report of the removal
accounts.gist: A crowd at the Roslyn depot threatened to lynch Alberson and Eato as they left for the county jail, and the Sheriff's officers had great difficulty getting them on the cars safely.

accounts.label: Officers' account of the case
accounts.gist: Footprints, boots, a bloodstained cloak, a confession by Eato and a pocketbook recovered from his cellar were reported as evidence against the men, all from the officers' side.

framing.detail: The Tribune mentioned the lynch threat in passing, without comment, inside an item on Valentine's recovery headed 'Removed to the Queens County Jail'.
Earlier Tribune items presented the men's guilt as near-certain ('No doubt is entertained of the guilt of Edward Alberson') and described them as 'negroes' of 'evil reputation'.
